694.title: How to keep reading
694.hook: you've read Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, the prophets, two gospels and three letters
694.howItsDone: Christians read the Bible in many ways: through a church lectionary, a yearly reading plan, or slow prayerful reading such as lectio divina, often in a small group or alongside their congregation's Sunday readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the elder's two short notes, and stoma, mouth to mouth. Your line was a tone, a hand on the shoulder.
screen: `A TONE, A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.`

segments.voice: A lesson a day opens one page. But the book on the shelf is thick, and some evenings you may want more: a psalm before bed, the rest of a story the lesson only touched. This year the lessons have walked from a garden in Genesis to a few short letters near the back of the book, and tomorrow they keep walking. Today is about reading on your own, and how Christians have kept this book open, alone and together.

Start with what kind of book it is. It isn't really one book; it's a library, written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek: poems, laws, letters, stories, songs and visions. Churches even shelve it a little differently: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles hold books that Protestant Bibles usually leave out or print in a separate section. So the first tip is a library's tip: you don't have to read the shelves in order. Some follow a lectionary, a set of readings for each day or each Sunday, so a whole congregation hears the same passage the same week; Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches, among others, use one. Some follow a reading plan, a few chapters a day, through the whole Bible in a year. And some read very slowly. The Rule of Saint Benedict sets aside hours for monks to give to lectio divina, holy reading. As it's often taught today, that means a short passage, read again and again, until one word catches and stays. The second tip: read with someone. The letter to the Colossians asks to be read aloud in church, then passed on to be read in the next town. A friend, a group or a church study keeps the book open. The third: some readers find it keeps surprising them. A psalm read young can sound different years later. From Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for your feet, not a floodlight for the whole road.
screen: `A LECTIONARY, A PLAN, A SLOW PAGE.`
then, large: `A LIGHT UNTO MY PATH.`

segments.voice: Think back over the year and notice which part pulled at you: the stories, perhaps Acts, the story of the first churches, or Ruth, which you can read in one sitting; the Psalms, one a day; or more of Jesus, in Mark, short and fast, or Matthew, with the Sermon on the Mount. Pick the one you'll actually open, and picture where and when: a chair, a time of day, a lamp. If you pray, ask for an open heart as you read.
Lectio divina. Holy reading, a short passage read again and again until one word catches and stays: one way among several to keep the book open.
Your line: the book keeps opening. One page, and then the next. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: Christmas: the Word again (John 1:14)
695.hook: at Christmas, churches read John's prologue: the Word became flesh
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book in your hands
695.howItsDone: In Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches, John 1:1–14 is read on Christmas Day and often as the last lesson at services of lessons and carols; Orthodox churches read Matthew's account of the Magi at the Nativity and John's prologue at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: how to keep reading, and lectio divina, holy reading. Your line was the book keeps opening.

Two Christmas readings, and they could hardly be more different. One is from Luke: shepherds, a manger, angels over the fields at night. The other is from John, and it has no manger at all. No shepherds, no star, no inn. It starts before time: in the beginning was the Word. In many churches, Luke's story is read at night, and John's opening on Christmas morning, or as the last reading at a candlelit service of lessons and carols. Today, the one verse in John that makes it a Christmas text.

John's Gospel opens the way Genesis does. In the King James Bible: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word, in Greek the logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind everything. Then: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." And the verse the passage leans toward, verse fourteen: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth." You met this verse in the autumn, through its tent: dwelt, in Greek, is pitched his tent. At Christmas, churches lean on the other word. Flesh. In Greek, sarx, the plain word for the stuff of bodies. John could have said the Word appeared, or visited. He says it became flesh. Not an idea, not a voice from the sky. At Christmas that flesh is a baby: someone who has to be fed, changed, carried and kept warm. Christians say the Word that was there in the beginning started out that small. Churches keep the day a little differently. Many celebrate on December twenty-fifth; many Orthodox churches that follow the older Julian calendar celebrate on what is now January seventh. Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches read this prologue on Christmas Day. In the Orthodox liturgy for the Nativity, the Gospel is Matthew's story of the Magi, and John's prologue is read at Easter. Luke tells you where he was born. John tells you who was born.
screen: `A BABY WHO HAS TO BE FED.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn the lights down, light one lamp or candle safely, and read John 1:1–14 slowly, looking at the flame for a breath when you reach the light shining in the darkness. When you reach the Word made flesh, think of one ordinary body you love, a hand, a face, a child asleep; Christians say God came that close. If you pray, read verse fourteen once more, slowly, as your prayer.
Christmas. The feast of the birth of Jesus, when John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and pitched his tent among us.
Your line: he dwelt among us. In John's telling, as close as flesh. See you tomorrow.

696.title: Year two close: the book in your hands
696.hook: a library you've walked through, from the garden to the shore at breakfast
696.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a favorite verse close, memorized, written in a Bible's margin or posted at home, and churches sometimes mark the end of a season of reading with a time of looking back and giving thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Christmas, and the Word made flesh. Your line was he dwelt among us.

This year began in a garden, where God walked in the cool of the day. Then a desert crossed by a whole people. A room full of songs, some joyful, some furious. Prophets shouting in the street. Then Luke and John, all the way to a charcoal fire on a beach at dawn where, in John's telling, the risen Jesus cooked breakfast for his friends. And lately, a few letters left on the table. Today is the last day of year two: one look back, and one verse to take with you.
screen: `A GARDEN, A DESERT, A ROOM OF SONGS.`

segments.voice: Year two had seven parts. Genesis: beginnings, a garden, a flood, a family that kept going wrong and kept being carried. Exodus: slaves, a sea, manna, a mountain, a golden calf, and long years in the wilderness. The Psalms and the wisdom books: prayers for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good. The prophets: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a king on a donkey. Luke: outsiders, meals and mercy. John: the Word, the signs, the bread and the light and the good shepherd, and that breakfast on the shore. And three letters of joy, faith and love: Philippians, James and First John, with the elder's two short notes. Now the verse. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives his last speeches before the people cross into the land without him. The commandment, he says, isn't hidden away. It isn't up in heaven, where someone would have to climb and fetch it, or across the sea, for someone to sail out and bring back. In the King James Bible: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Very nigh. The Hebrew word is karov: close by, within reach. Paul later quoted this line in his letter to the Romans: "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart." Jewish and Christian tradition each read the verse in its own way, but the picture is shared: the word isn't a far-off mountain only experts can climb. It's near enough to say, and to keep. After a year of reading, the book is in your hands.
screen: `NOT IN HEAVEN, NOT ACROSS THE SEA.`
then, large: `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.`

segments.voice: Let the year go past and ask which verse stayed: maybe the Lord is my shepherd, a line from a prophet, no fear in love, or something small nobody else would pick. Choose the one already near you, not the most famous, and if you can, write it down by hand. If you pray, give thanks for a year of reading.
Karov. Hebrew for near, close by: the word Moses said wasn't far off in heaven or across the sea, but near enough to say, and to keep.
Your line: the word is near you. Tomorrow, year three begins with Joshua. Year two, done.

697.title: Be strong and courageous (Joshua 1:1–9)
697.hook: Moses is gone, and Joshua is told three times: be strong, don't be afraid
697.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Joshua 1:9 before a hard new beginning, such as a move, a new job or an exam, and some memorize it or keep it written where they will see it.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed year two with karov: the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. Now year three begins.

"Moses my servant is dead." That is how God's first words to Joshua in this book begin. No easing in. Moses stood before Pharaoh, went up the mountain, spoke with God for everyone. Joshua was his assistant; the opening verse calls him "Moses' minister." Now the people are camped by the Jordan River, the land is on the far side, and the one who always seemed to know what came next is gone. The same sentence moves on: "now therefore arise, go over this Jordan." And before Joshua takes a single step, God tells him the same thing again, and again.

Year three is the long story: Israel after the wilderness, from Joshua to the return from exile. It opens with a handover. In nine verses, God tells Joshua three times to be strong. In the King James Bible, verse six: "Be strong and of a good courage." Verse seven pushes further: "Only be thou strong and very courageous." Verse nine makes it a question: "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." Some readers notice that people rarely need telling three times unless something in them is shaking. The text never says what Joshua felt. It only gives him the words. Now look where the courage comes from. Each reason points away from Joshua. Verse five: "as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee." The strength rests on company, not on confidence. And there's a surprise tucked in the middle. Verse eight ties the command to a book: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night." The first thing asked of a new leader about to cross a river is to keep reading. Some Christians turn to this chapter at new starts. The line to carry is the quiet one in verse five: I will not fail thee.
screen: then, large: `I WILL NOT FAIL THEE, NOR FORSAKE THEE.`

segments.voice: Let one small, real thing come to mind that you've been putting off because it unsettles you a little: a phone call, an apology, a first page. Don't solve it; just name it, and sit with the words Joshua heard: be strong, be not afraid. If you pray, hold that one thing up and rest on the promise, I will not fail thee; if you don't, simply breathe with it.
Chazak. Hebrew for be strong: what God tells Joshua three times as Moses' work passes into his hands, courage resting on company, not on confidence.
Your line: I will not fail you. Courage that rests on company, not confidence. Year three, day one.

698.title: Rahab's scarlet cord (Joshua 2)
698.hook: a woman on the city wall hides two spies and hangs a red cord from her window
698.howItsDone: Christians meet Rahab in sermons on Hebrews 11 and on welcoming outsiders, and some churches teach the scarlet cord as a sign of rescue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chazak: be strong, and your line was I will not fail you.

A red line hangs from a window in a city wall. Joshua has sent two men across the river to spy out Jericho, and in the King James words they "came into an harlot's house, named Rahab, and lodged there." Her house is built into the town wall. The king hears that spies are inside, and his men come to her door. Rahab has already hidden the spies on her roof, under stalks of flax. She tells them the strangers left at dark: hurry, and you'll catch them.
screen: `TWO SPIES, ONE HOUSE IN THE WALL.`

segments.voice: Rahab gives her reason, and it's an outsider's confession. Her city has heard what Israel's God has done, and their hearts have melted. Then, in the King James Bible: "for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath." Those words echo, almost exactly, what Moses tells Israel in Deuteronomy. A Canaanite woman, in a city about to fall, speaks Israel's own creed back to Israel's spies. Then she asks for one thing. The Hebrew word is chesed: loyal kindness. I showed you kindness; show kindness to my father's house. Spare my parents, my brothers, my sisters. The spies agree. She lets them down from her window by a cord, and they tell her: "thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by." Everyone inside will be safe. Then, as soon as they're gone: "And she bound the scarlet line in the window." She doesn't wait for the army. She hangs the sign of the promise while nothing has happened yet, and lives under it. Some Christian readers see the thread as a picture of rescue through blood, like the blood on the doorposts at Passover. Others see a woman staking her family on a promise from strangers. The story doesn't end at Jericho. Hebrews names her: "By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace." James praises what she did. Matthew's family line of Jesus includes a Rachab, traditionally taken to be her. The woman on the wall ends up inside the story.
screen: `SHE TIES IT BEFORE THE ARMY COMES.`

segments.voice: Rahab's risk was her life; yours can be smaller: speaking up for someone being talked about, sitting with the person nobody sits with, siding out loud with the unpopular one. Let one person come to mind who could use someone on their side, and ask what it would cost you to help. If you pray, hold them up by name; if not, keep them in mind and breathe.
Chesed. Hebrew for loyal kindness: what Rahab asked the spies to answer, the kindness she had shown them, with kindness for her family.
Your line: the cord in the window. She tied it before anything had happened. See you tomorrow.

699.title: Twelve stones (Joshua 3–4)
699.hook: the Jordan parts, and they pile stones so their children will ask what they mean
699.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a stone, a cross or another small object as a reminder of a time they believe God carried them through, and some families make a habit of telling those stories to their children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chesed: loyal kindness, and your line was the cord in the window.

"What mean ye by these stones?" That question is the reason for today's story, and nobody has asked it yet. The people stand at the Jordan, and the river is not low: it "overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest." Joshua tells the priests to carry the ark of the covenant to the edge. Not to wait. To walk in. Their feet touch the water, and upstream the river rises up in a heap. The priests stand on dry ground in the riverbed while all the people pass over. Then Joshua gives an odd order: go back in, and pick up some rocks.

One man from each of the twelve tribes takes a stone on his shoulder, from where the priests stood. Before anyone lifts one, Joshua tells them why, in the King James Bible: "That this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?" The answer is a story: the waters were cut off before the ark. They carry them to Gilgal, where Joshua sets them up. The text mentions no writing on them. They're a heap of river rocks in a strange place, and that's the point. They're built to make a child stop and ask. A memorial that works only when someone asks, and someone else tells the story. The chapter says it again near the end: "Then ye shall let your children know, saying, Israel came over this Jordan on dry land." In between is a stranger detail. Verse nine says Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the river, where the priests had stood, "and they are there unto this day." One pile on the bank, where anyone can see it. Another in the riverbed, under the water once it flows again. The text never explains the second pile. Some readers hear a reminder that part of what carries a person stays out of sight. And the chapter's last verse widens the circle: it was done so "that all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD."
screen: `A STONE FROM WHERE THE PRIESTS STOOD.`

segments.voice: Look for something that marks a time you were carried through: a ring, a card, a hospital bracelet, a chipped mug, or one that comes to mind. Hold it, or picture it, and ask what story it would tell if a child picked it up and said, what's this? If you pray, give thanks for the river you crossed; if you don't, simply hold the memory and breathe.
Twelve stones. River rocks set up at Gilgal, so that children would ask what they mean and hear the story.
Your line: what do these stones mean? Some memorials only work when someone asks. Day six hundred ninety-nine, done.

700.title: The walls of Jericho (Joshua 6)
700.hook: seven days of marching, trumpets, a shout; readers across traditions wrestle honestly with the violence of the conquest stories
700.tomorrow: As for me and my house
700.howItsDone: Christians read Joshua 6 in different ways, as ancient history, as a picture of spiritual struggle, or beside texts that push against it, and some Bible study groups take time to discuss its violence openly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve stones from the river, and your line: what do these stones mean?

"Ye shall not shout, nor make any noise with your voice, neither shall any word proceed out of your mouth." That is Joshua's order to an army. Not sharpen your swords. Be quiet. Jericho is shut up tight. Once a day for six days, Israel walks around the city: armed men, then seven priests blowing trumpets of rams' horns, then the ark, and not one word. On the seventh day they circle it seven times. The priests blow, the people shout with a great shout, and the text says the wall fell down flat. But the chapter doesn't stop when the wall falls.

The verse after the shout, in the King James Bible: "And they utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, and sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword." Read slowly, it's hard to hear. The Hebrew word behind it is cherem: something devoted to God and taken out of ordinary use, which in war meant destruction. The King James renders it accursed. Jews and Christians have both lived with this chapter, in different ways. Some read it as history: a brutal practice of the ancient world, told plainly, not a pattern for today. Some Christian teachers have read the battles as a picture of an inner war against greed, pride and fear. Some read the conquest beside the parts of the Bible that push against it, and the text itself pushes. In this very chapter, the one household spared is Canaanite: Rahab's, under the red line. And just before the march, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword and asks, "Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?" The answer: "Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come." Joshua falls on his face. God is not simply drafted onto Israel's side; Joshua is the one asked to bow. None of these readings makes it easy. Wrestling with a hard text out loud is one honest way to read scripture, and Genesis has a picture of it: Jacob wrestles through the night until daybreak, and comes away blessed, and limping.

If you can, walk once around your block or your room without a word; if you can't, sit and let your attention move slowly along the edges of the space. Bring to mind one hard passage and don't solve, defend or dismiss it: just walk around it quietly, the way Israel walked around a wall. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is.
Cherem. Hebrew for devoted, set apart for God and taken out of ordinary use: the word behind Jericho's destruction.
Your line: wrestle with hard texts. Not skip them, not settle them too fast. That's day seven hundred.
